why:
FINAL. Most signals are clean, but one is not, and it is not explainable as noise.

Clean evidence: over 120 s / 9788 requests, canary 1.1 served 2384 requests with 0 5xx (0.00% err), identical to stable 1.0 (7404 requests, 0 5xx). p50 and p95 match everywhere: overall 33/95 canary vs 35/95 stable; /browse 22/27 vs 22/27; /search 47/60 vs 47/59; /checkout 79/102 vs 82/103 (canary marginally faster on checkout). The four 30 s windows are flat with no drift or error onset (canary p95 95/95/92/95 vs stable 96/93/94/97, 0 5xx in every window).

The disqualifying signal: canary /search p99 = 652 ms vs stable /search p99 = 61 ms, a ~10x tail regression, which also lifts canary overall p99 to 172 ms vs stable 104 ms.

Why I do not dismiss it as a single outlier: p99 over 729 canary /search requests sits at roughly the 722nd ordered value, so about 7-8 requests (~1%) are at or above ~650 ms. If version 1.0 had the same ~1% tail, stable /search, with 2273 requests (3x the sample), would show a p99 in the hundreds of ms as well; it shows 61 ms. So the slow tail is specific to build 1.1 on one endpoint, not a sampling artifact.

What the dashboard cannot tell me (judgement): the over-time table reports only p95, not p99, so I cannot distinguish a one-off warm-up / cold-cache burst on a freshly started pod from a sustained ~1% regression in search. Eight slow requests inside a 30 s window would not visibly move an all-endpoint p95, so the flat p95 timeline neither confirms nor clears it.

Decision rule (judgement): the costs are asymmetric. Promoting pushes an unexplained 10x tail regression on a user-facing endpoint from 25% to 100% of traffic; rolling back only delays a release and is fully reversible. An unexplained canary-only regression is not a pass. Rollback, then re-run the canary with per-window p99 and per-endpoint traces for /search, excluding pod warm-up from the measurement window; if the 650 ms tail is confined to the first requests after start, promote on the next run.
